title: turn down the volume
subtitle: a precise word can calm a loud feeling

steps.prompt: what small frame puts distance around a thought?

steps.text: when a feeling is loud, giving it a precise name can help turn the volume down.
it sounds almost too simple. here's where it comes from.
in a 2007 brain imaging study at ucla, putting a feeling into words quieted the amygdala, part of the brain's alarm system. researchers call it affect labeling.
what's one feeling you've had today?

options.label: good
options.reply: nice. naming the good ones counts too.

options.label: tired
options.reply: noted. just naming it is the practice.

options.label: worried
options.reply: noted. just naming it is the practice.

options.label: annoyed
options.reply: noted. just naming it is the practice.

steps.text: most of us lean on a few big words: fine. bad. stressed. there are a lot more.

steps.prompt: which of these could fit a "stressed" day?
steps.reply: precise words like these are linked to coping better. researchers call it emotion differentiation.

steps.prompt: same feeling, three volumes. try each one on:
steps.reply: each one is true in different moments. the precise one helps everyone know where things are, inside included.

steps.prompt: now one good feeling from today, with its volume. this one goes in the book:
ideas: kind of excited about the weekend.

steps.text: a precise word for a feeling can help turn its volume down.

source.label: Lieberman et al., 2007; Kashdan et al., 2015

steps.text: today, when you'd say "fine", find one more precise word.

grounding.idea: putting feelings into words reduced amygdala response
telling feelings apart precisely is linked to healthier coping
